A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PICABU in Causal Climate Emulation with Bayesian Filtering. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and can be matched across revisions and relocations.

before.justification: v1 reports original SAVAR causal-recovery experiments, NorESM2 and CESM2-FV2 emulation, generalization tests, ablations, and a counterfactual case study.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds filter-variance comparisons and quantitative intervention analyses in Appendices J, P, and Q.

M1.justification: Section 4.4 adds observation-space interventions that perturb temperature grid cells before encoding and prediction, alongside the retained latent-space intervention procedure. The architecture, training losses, and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged; constant filter variance was already specified in v1.

E1.justification: The datasets, emissions scenarios, and multivariable emulation coverage are retained. Counterfactual coverage expands from the ENSO latent intervention to observation-space perturbations of ENSO, the Indian Ocean Dipole, and Alaska, including Australian temperature responses.

E2.justification: CDSD, V-PCMCI, and ViT with positional encoding retain their comparison roles in Tables 1–5. New Table 6 adds an internal comparator using model-inferred filter variance against PICABU's default constant variance.

E3.justification: Existing benchmark splits, inputs, metrics, and training settings are retained. New protocols compare filter-variance choices and quantify responses across intervention magnitudes. Appendix P specifies two-standard-deviation perturbations for Niño3.4 and Alaska and a 0.5 increase in the IOD index.

E4.justification: Validation expands substantially beyond v1's qualitative ENSO intervention example: Appendix P adds quantitative regional interventions and an Alaskan control, while Appendix Q checks the latent-to-temperature relationship. Appendix J independently ablates the filter's variance choice. Earlier component and sensitivity analyses remain present.

E5.justification: The ten-rollout spectral mean/standard-deviation reporting and Table 3 t-tests are retained. v2 clarifies the t-test reference as PICABU without changing the procedure. New intervention correlations lack uncertainty intervals; the disclosed 100 tuning runs are hyperparameter trials, not repeated evaluations for uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Tables 1–5 retain their values, but substantial new intervention and variance-comparison results are reported. Appendices P–Q add correlations of 0.90 for ENSO–GMST, 0.87 for IOD–Australian temperature, 0.08 for Alaska–GMST, and 0.98 for latent–temperature correspondence. Table 6 reports mixed variance-choice effects: inferred variance worsens GMST standard deviation from 0.277 to 0.324, but improves IOD LSD from 0.0772 to 0.0753.

T1.justification: Equations 1–15, the CDSD formulation, single-parent assumptions, and Bayesian-filter mathematics are retained. The new variance rationale and illustration of the existing Beta(4,8) distribution introduce no new formal assumptions, derivations, or proofs.

C1.justification: Both versions claim interpretable causal climate emulation, stable Bayesian-filtered rollouts, improved generalization, and counterfactual capability. Replacing 'physics-informed losses' with 'additional losses' changes terminology without substantively changing these claimed capabilities.

C2.justification: v2 explains the single-parent representation through an analogy with regional climate indices, motivates constant variance as limiting excess modeled variability, and interprets the new interventions through expected teleconnections. Existing limitations concerning single-parent decoding, high-frequency variability, and anthropogenic forcing remain.

D1.justification: Appendices N–O newly disclose a 100-run search over 20 parameters and rollout timing below six minutes per simulated century on one RTX8000, including batching and scaling details. Intervention magnitudes are specified, and the stated SAVAR license changes from CC BY 4.0 to GPLv3. Existing hyperparameter values and data access information are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds Boussard et al. (2023) on causal climate representations and Cai et al. (2009) on IOD-related Australian impacts. It also expands the positioning of single-parent latents relative to conventional climate indices; the broader related-work framework is retained.

P1.justification: There are targeted explanatory expansions in Sections 2.1 and 3.3, a revised intervention narrative in Section 4.4, and additional appendix subsections. Copyediting, loss terminology, affiliations, and the conference header also change, while the overall organization and most existing prose remain.

P2.justification: v2 adds focused displays for the SAVAR link distribution, observation-space interventions, intervention correlations, and filter-variance comparison. v1 Figure 10 moves into the main text as Figure 4, and v1 Figure 4 is retained as Figure 25. Most existing graphics and table formats remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: The variance ablation and quantitative intervention checks provide useful support beyond v1's design description and qualitative counterfactual example. Runtime and tuning disclosures also improve transparency. These are targeted gains: variance effects are mixed, and the new interventions remain demonstrations within the learned emulator without independent counterfactual validation or reported uncertainty.
